nodes.statement: Any Whittaker module V of type psi that admits a central character chi: Z(g)->C is a quotient of a universal module Y_{chi,psi}=U(g) otimes_{Z(g)U(n)} C*w_{chi,psi}, where Z(g)U(n)=Z(g) otimes U(n) acts on the 1-dimensional space C*w_{chi,psi} by chi otimes psi.
nodes.raw_latex:
Any Whittaker module $V$ of type $\psi$ that admits a central character $\chi:\ Z(\fg)\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ is a quotient of a universal module
  $$\mathcal{Y}_{\chi,\psi}=U(\fg)\ot_{Z(\fg)U(\mf{n})}\mathbb{C}w_{\chi,\psi},$$
  where $Z(\fg)U(\mf{n})=Z(\fg)\ot U(\mf{n})$ acts on the $1$-dimensional space $\mathbb{C}w_{\chi,\psi}$ by $\chi\ot\psi$.

nodes.statement: Let psi: eta -> C be the Whittaker character of V. The module V has an obvious filtration V = union_{k=0}^infty V^(k), where V^(k) = {v in V: x_0 bullet x_1 bullet ... bullet x_k bullet v = 0 for all x_0, x_1, ..., x_k in n}, and x bullet v is defined as xv - psi(x)v for all x in n and v in V. Let v be a nonzero element of V. If v not in Wh V, then x bullet v != 0 for some x in n. But x bullet v in V^(k-1) whenever v in V^(k), so V^(0) cap U(g)v != 0. If Wh V is 1-dimensional and spanned by a vector w, then by definition, V^(0) = Wh V = Cw and V = U(g)w. In this case, we see that Cw = V^(0) subseteq U(g)v. Since w generates V, the module V is thus simple when Wh V is 1-dimensional. Conversely, by McDowell's classification, any simple Whittaker module is of the form L_{Omega,psi} for some Whittaker character psi: n -> C and central character Omega in Z(l_psi)^*. The centre z of the Lie algebra l = l_psi acts semisimply on Y_{Omega,psi}. Since z subseteq h, it also acts semisimply on the induced module M_{Omega,psi} = U(g) otimes_{U(p)} Y_{Omega,psi} and on its simple quotient L_{Omega,psi}. That is, M_{Omega,psi} = bigoplus_{mu in z^*} M_{Omega,psi}^mu and L_{Omega,psi} = bigoplus_{mu in z^*} L_{Omega,psi}^mu, where V^mu = {v in V: hv = mu(h)v for all h in z} for any g-module V. Since z acts on Y_{Omega,psi} by the restriction Omega-bar of the character Omega to z, it acts on M_{Omega,psi} = U(m-bar) otimes_C U(p) otimes_{U(p)} Y_{Omega,psi} = U(m-bar) otimes_C Y_{Omega,psi} by weights bounded above by Omega-bar. Similarly, L_{Omega,psi} = bigoplus_{mu preceq Omega-bar} L_{Omega,psi}^mu. Let v be a Whittaker vector in L_{Omega,psi}, with decomposition v = sum_{mu preceq Omega-bar} v_mu relative to (REF). Let x in n = l_+ oplus m be a root vector in a root space g_alpha. If x in l_+, then z commutes with x and xL_{Omega,psi}^mu subseteq L_{Omega,psi}^mu. In particular, sum_mu psi(x)v_mu = xv = sum_mu xv_mu, so by comparing graded components, xv_mu = psi(x)v_mu for all mu. If x in m, then zx = x(z + alpha(z)), for all z in z, so xL_{Omega,psi}^mu subseteq L_{Omega,psi}^{mu+alpha-bar}, where alpha-bar is the restriction of alpha to z. But psi vanishes on m by construction, so 0 = xv = sum_{mu preceq Omega-bar} xv_mu. Each xv_mu belongs to a distinct graded component, so xv_mu = 0 for all mu. The subalgebras l_+ and m are spanned by root vectors, so xv_mu = psi(x)v_mu for all x in n and mu preceq Omega-bar. That is, v_mu in Wh V for all mu. Let mu prec Omega-bar. Then by degree considerations, the submodule U(g)v_mu = U(m-bar oplus l)v_mu subseteq sum_{lambda preceq mu} L_{Omega,psi}^lambda is proper in L_{Omega,psi}. As L_{Omega,psi} is simple, we see that v_mu = 0 and v = v_{Omega-bar}. Therefore, v is a Whittaker vector in the simple s-Whittaker module Y_{Omega,psi} = L_{Omega,psi}^{Omega-bar} of type psi-bar, where psi-bar is the restriction of psi to the positive part l_+ of s = [l,l]. As Y_{Omega,psi} is non-singular, Kostant's criterion applies, and its space W of Whittaker vectors is 1-dimensional. The space Wh L_{Omega,psi} subseteq W is thus also 1-dimensional.

\proof Let $\psi:\ \eta\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be the Whittaker character of $V$.  The module $V$ has an obvious filtration $V=\bigcup_{k=0}^\infty V^{(k)}$, where
  $$V^{(k)}=\{v\in V:\ x_0\bullet x_1\bullet\cdots\bullet x_k\bullet v=0\hbox{\ for all\ }x_0,x_1,\ldots ,x_k\in\mathfrak{n}\},$$
  and $x\bullet v$ is defined as $xv-\psi(x)v$ for all $x\in\mathfrak{n}$ and $v\in V$. 

  Let $v$ be a nonzero element of $V$.  If $v\notin\hbox{Wh}\,V$, then $x\bullet v\neq0$ for some $x\in\mathfrak{n}$.  But $x\bullet v\in V^{(k-1)}$ whenever $v\in V^{(k)}$, so $V^{(0)}\cap U(\fg)v\neq 0$.   If $\hbox{Wh}\,V$ is $1$-dimensional and spanned by a vector $w$, then by definition, $V^{(0)}=\hbox{Wh}\,V=\mathbb{C}w$ and $V=U(\mathfrak{g})w$.  In this case, we see that $\mathbb{C}w= V^{(0)}\subseteq U(\fg)v$.  Since $w$ generates $V$, the module $V$ is thus simple when $\hbox{Wh}\,V$ is $1$-dimensional.

  Conversely, by McDowell's classification, any simple Whittaker module is of the form $L_{\Omega,\psi}$ for some Whittaker character $\psi:\ \mathfrak{n}\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ and central character $\Omega\in Z(\mathfrak{l}_\psi)^*$.  The centre $\mathfrak{z}$ of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{l}=\mathfrak{l}_\psi$ acts semisimply on $Y_{\Omega,\psi}$.  Since $\mathfrak{z}\subseteq\mathfrak{h}$, it also acts semisimply on the induced module $M_{\Omega,\psi}=U(\mathfrak{g})\ot_{U(\mathfrak{p})}Y_{\Omega,\psi}$ and on its simple quotient $L_{\Omega,\psi}$.  That is,
  $$M_{\Omega,\psi}=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\mathfrak{z}^*}M_{\Omega,\psi}^\mu\hbox{\ and\ }L_{\Omega,\psi}=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\mathfrak{z}^*}L_{\Omega,\psi}^\mu,$$
  where $V^\mu=\{v\in V\ :\ hv=\mu(h)v\hbox{\ for all\ }h\in\mathfrak{z}\}$ for any $\fg$-module $V$.  Since $\mathfrak{z}$ acts on $Y_{\Omega,\psi}$ by the restriction $\overline{\Omega}$ of the character $\Omega$ to $\mathfrak{z}$, it acts on
  $$M_{\Omega,\psi}=U(\overline{\mf{m}})\ot_\mathbb{C}U(\mf{p})\ot_{U(\mf{p})}Y_{\Omega,\psi}=U(\overline{\mf{m}})\ot_\mathbb{C} Y_{\Omega,\psi}$$
  by weights bounded above by $\overline{\Omega}$.  Similarly, 
\begin{equation}\label{star}
  L_{\Omega,\psi}=\bigoplus_{\mu\preceq\overline{\Omega}}L_{\Omega,\psi}^\mu.
\end{equation}

Let $v$ be a Whittaker vector in $L_{\Omega,\psi}$, with decomposition $v=\sum_{\mu\preceq\overline{\Omega}}v_\mu$ relative to (\ref{star}).  Let $x\in\mf{n}=\mf{l}_+\oplus\mf{m}$ be a root vector in a root space $\fg_\ga$.  If $x\in\mf{l}_+$, then $\mf{z}$ commutes with $x$ and $xL_{\Omega,\psi}^\mu\subseteq L_{\Omega,\psi}^\mu$.  In particular, $\sum_\mu\psi(x)v_\mu=xv=\sum_\mu xv_\mu$, so by comparing graded components, $xv_\mu=\psi(x)v_\mu$ for all $\mu$.  If $x\in\mf{m}$, then
$$zx=x(z+\ga(z)),$$
for all $z\in\mf{z}$, so
$$xL_{\Omega,\psi}^\mu\subseteq L_{\Omega,\psi}^{\mu+\overline{\ga}},$$
where $\overline{\ga}$ is the restriction of $\ga$ to $\mf{z}$.  But $\psi$ vanishes on $\mf{m}$ by construction, so
$$0=xv=\sum_{\mu\preceq\overline{\Omega}}xv_\mu.$$
Each $xv_\mu$ belongs to a distinct graded component, so $xv_\mu=0$ for all $\mu$.  The subalgebras $\mf{l}_+$ and $\mf{m}$ are spanned by root vectors, so $xv_\mu=\psi(x)v_\mu$ for all $x\in\mf{n}$ and $\mu\preceq\overline{\Omega}$.  That is, $v_\mu\in\hbox{Wh}\,V$ for all $\mu$.

Let $\mu\prec\overline{\Omega}$.  Then by degree considerations, the submodule
$$U(\fg)v_\mu=U(\overline{\mf{m}}\oplus\mf{l})v_\mu\subseteq\sum_{\lambda\preceq\mu}L_{\Omega,\psi}^\lambda$$
is proper in $L_{\Omega,\psi}$.  As $L_{\Omega,\psi}$ is simple, we see that $v_\mu=0$ and $v=v_{\overline{\Omega}}$.  Therefore, $v$ is a Whittaker vector in the simple $\mf{s}$-Whittaker module $Y_{\Omega,\psi}=L_{\Omega,\psi}^{\overline{\Omega}}$ of type $\overline{\psi}$, where $\overline{\psi}$ is the restriction of $\psi$ to the positive part $\mf{l}_+$ of $\mf{s}=[\mf{l},\mf{l}]$.  As $Y_{\Omega,\psi}$ is non-singular, Kostant's criterion \cite[Theorem 3.6.1]{kostant78} applies, and its space $W$ of Whittaker vectors is $1$-dimensional.  The space $\hbox{Wh}\,L_{\Omega,\psi}\subseteq W$ is thus also $1$-dimensional.\qed

nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we may assume that M is of finite length and has a composition series 0 = M_0 subset M_1 subset ... subset M_ell = M. We induct on the length ell of M, and as the base case ell = 0 is trivial, we may assume that ell > 0. For any i > 0 and nonzero m in M_i/M_{i-1}, the Lie subalgebra n acts on the finite dimensional space U(n)m. By Lie's theorem, U(n)m subseteq M_i/M_{i-1} contains a nonzero Whittaker vector n, and by simplicity M_i/M_{i-1} = U(g)n is thus a Whittaker module. The space Wh(M_i/M_{i-1}) is 1-dimensional by Theorem REF. If v, w in M are nonzero Whittaker vectors, then their images v + M_{ell-1} and w + M_{ell-1} lie in the 1-dimensional space Wh(M_ell/M_{ell-1}). The vector v is thus of the form lambda w + u for some lambda in C and u in M_{ell-1}. As u = v - lambda w is clearly also a Whittaker vector and dim Wh(M_{ell-1}) <= ell - 1 by induction, it follows that dim Wh M <= 1 + dim Wh(M_{ell-1}) <= ell.
nodes.raw_latex:
\proof Without loss of generality, we may assume that $M$ is of finite length and has a composition series
$$0=M_0\subset M_1\subset\cdots\subset M_\ell=M.$$
We induct on the length $\ell$ of $M$, and as the base case $\ell=0$ is trivial, we may assume that $\ell>0$.

For any $i>0$ and nonzero $m\in M_i/M_{i-1}$, the Lie subalgebra $\mf{n}$ acts on the finite dimensional space $U(\mf{n})m$.  By Lie's theorem, $U(\mf{n})m\subseteq M_i/M_{i-1}$ contains a nonzero Whittaker vector $n$, and by simplicity $M_i/M_{i-1}=U(\fg)n$ is thus a Whittaker module.  The space $\hbox{Wh}(M_i/M_{i-1})$ is $1$-dimensional by Theorem \ref{mainthm}.

If $v,w\in M$ are nonzero Whittaker vectors, then their images $v+M_{\ell-1}$ and $w+M_{\ell-1}$ lie in the $1$-dimensional space $\hbox{Wh}(M_\ell/M_{\ell-1})$. The vector $v$ is thus of the form $\lambda w + u$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$ and $u\in M_{\ell-1}$.  As $u=v-\lambda w$ is clearly also a Whittaker vector and $\dim\hbox{Wh}(M_{\ell-1})\leq \ell-1$ by induction, it follows that $\dim\hbox{Wh}\,M\leq 1+\dim\hbox{Wh}(M_{\ell-1})\leq\ell.$\qed

nodes.statement: The module M_Omega,psi has a unique simple quotient L_Omega,psi, and every simple Whittaker module of type psi is isomorphic to a module L_Omega,psi for some character Omega: Z(l)->C.
nodes.raw_latex: {\em \cite[Theorem 2.9]{mcdowell85}}  The module $M_{\Omega,\psi}$ has a unique simple quotient $L_{\Omega,\psi}$, and every simple Whittaker module of type $\psi$ is isomorphic to a module $L_{\Omega,\psi}$ for some character $\Omega:\ Z(\mathfrak{l})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$.\qed

nodes.statement: Let V be a Whittaker module for fg. Then V is simple if and only if WhV is 1-dimensional.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{mainthm}
Let $V$ be a Whittaker module for $\fg$.  Then $V$ is simple if and only if $\hbox{Wh}\,V$ is $1$-dimensional.
nodes.clean_text: Let V be a Whittaker module for fg. Then V is simple if and only if WhV is 1-dimensional.
